# Introduction

## Background

Globally, extreme weather events such as floods, cold waves, droughts and heatwaves have become increasingly frequent and intense[@ebi2021]. These events disrupt multiple sectors including energy infrastructure, agriculture, food production, healthcare and livelihoods, resulting in substantial social and economic losses [@zhang2023; @costello2009]. Consistent with these changes, global mean near-surface temperatures have risen by approximately 1.4–1.5°C above pre-industrial (1850–1900) levels, with the five-year average temperature during 2020–2025 being the highest on record and 2024 recorded as the warmest year globally [@adriansimmons2021]. This continued warming is largely driven by increasing greenhouse gas emissions, together with changes and interactions in atmospheric and oceanic circulation [@change2022; @adriansimmons2021]. One of the most direct consequences of rising global temperatures is the increasing occurrence of heatwaves, commonly defined as periods of unusually high temperatures that persist for several consecutive days. Climate projections indicate that both the frequency and intensity of heatwaves will continue to increase unless substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions are accompanied by investments in climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure [@change2022].

Heatwaves have important implications for both population health and the delivery of healthcare services. Extreme heat places additional pressure on health systems through increased demand for healthcare, disruptions to essential services, and challenges in maintaining critical infrastructure. At the individual level, heat exposure has been associated with an increased incidence of heat-related illnesses and injuries, particularly among older adults, prolonged recovery among hospitalized patients, increased in-patient mortality, and excess mortality across many regions of the world [@hajat2007; @ferron2006; @stafoggia2008; @hundessa2025; @clarke2025; @he]. Heatwaves may also compromise the storage and transport of temperature-sensitive medical products, including vaccines, medicines and medical equipment, by placing additional strain on cold-chain systems [@curtis2017; @carmichael2012]. These impacts increase pressure on already constrained healthcare systems and have the potential to disrupt the delivery of essential public health services, including routine childhood immunization.

Nigeria has experienced several notable heatwave events in recent decades, including those occurring in 2002, 2019, 2020, 2023 and 2024 [@adefisan2018; @morakinyo2024; @climate2025]. These events have been linked to broader climatic changes, compounded by rapid urbanisation, deforestation and land-use change. Their impacts have been felt across multiple sectors. In agriculture, the 2024 heatwave was associated with an estimated 20% decline in agricultural production in a country where food production depends heavily on rainfall [@oluwaseun2024; @climate2025]. Heatwaves have also increased pressure on Nigeria's energy infrastructure through higher cooling demand, contributing to electricity shortages and national grid failures [@oluwaseun2024]. In the health sector, they have been associated with increased occurrence of heat-related illnesses such as heat stroke and meningitis, while environmentally they have contributed to increased wildfire risk and the progression of desertification, particularly in northern Nigeria [@oluwaseun2024; @gbadegesin2011].

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Nigeria's National Programme on Immunization (NPI) was established in 1978 to provide routine immunization services for children. Over the years, the programme has expanded to include additional vaccine antigens in line with the country's Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI). According to the current national immunization schedule (Table 1.1), a child is considered fully immunized upon receiving one dose of Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG), the hepatitis B birth dose, four doses of oral polio vaccine (OPV), two doses of inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), three doses each of the pentavalent, pneumococcal conjugate (PCV) and rotavirus vaccines, two doses of measles-containing vaccine (MCV), and one dose each of the yellow fever and meningitis vaccines [@ndhs].

```{r tbl-meth}
vaccines <- tibble(
  Time = c(
    rep("At birth", 3),
    rep("6 weeks", 5),
    rep("10 weeks", 4),
    rep("14 weeks", 5),
    "6 months",
    rep("9 months", 3),
    "12 months",
    "15 months"
  ),
  Vaccine = c(
    "BCG",
    "OPV 0 (Birth dose)",
    "Hepatitis B birth dose",
    
    "Pentavalent (DPT, Hepatitis B, HiB) 1",
    "Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine 1",
    "OPV 1 (1st dose)",
    "Rotavirus 1",
    "IPV1",
    
    "Pentavalent (DPT, Hepatitis B, HiB) 2",
    "Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine 2",
    "OPV 2 (2nd dose)",
    "Rotavirus 2",
    
    "Pentavalent (DPT, Hepatitis B, HiB) 3",
    "Pneumococcal Conjugate Vaccine 3",
    "OPV 3 (3rd dose)",
    "Rotavirus 3",
    "IPV2",
    
    "Vitamin A (1st dose)",
    
    "Measles 1st dose (MCV1)",
    "Yellow Fever",
    "Meningitis Vaccine",
    
    "Vitamin A (2nd dose)",
    
    "Measles 2nd dose (MCV2)"
  )
)

vaccines |>
  kbl(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Minimum target age", "Vaccine"),
    align = c("l", "l"),
    linesep = ""
  ) |>
  collapse_rows(
    columns = 1,
    valign = "middle"
  ) |>
  kable_classic(
    full_width = FALSE,
    html_font = "Times New Roman"
  ) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "2.2cm", bold = TRUE) |>
  column_spec(2, width = "7cm") |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE)
```

Despite substantial progress over recent decades, routine childhood immunization coverage in Nigeria remains below both national and global targets and continues to be characterised by marked geographical and socioeconomic disparities [@williams2024; @ogunniyi2024]. Although the proportion of children receiving all basic vaccinations increased from 13% in 2003 to 39% in 2024, coverage remains considerably lower in northern Nigeria than in the southern regions [@ndhs; @ophori2014; @alabi2024]. These inequalities have been associated with several factors, including place of delivery, maternal education, household wealth, and urban–rural residence [@ndhs; @alabi2024; @salako2024]. Consequently, Nigeria continues to account for a substantial proportion of the global burden of undervaccinated children [@ogunniyi2024]. Persistent challenges facing the national immunization programme include supply chain constraints, shortages of healthcare personnel and funding, limited geographical access to health facilities, and vaccine hesitancy driven by sociocultural and religious factors [@ogunniyi2024; @watch2023]. More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted routine immunization services, slowing progress towards improving vaccination coverage and access [@adegoke2024].

Although vaccination coverage remains the most commonly reported indicator of immunization program performance, it does not capture whether vaccines are administered at the recommended ages [@umeokonkwo; @derqui2024]. Vaccination timeliness refers to the administration of vaccines within the age windows specified by the national immunization schedule [@macdonald2018]. Unlike coverage, which only measures whether a child has eventually received a vaccine, timeliness distinguishes between early, timely and delayed vaccination. This distinction is important because vaccines administered too early may result in reduced vaccine effectiveness owing to interference from maternal antibodies or an immature infant immune system [@hughes2020; @goult2024], while delayed vaccination prolongs children's susceptibility to vaccine-preventable diseases during periods of greatest risk and has been associated with disease outbreaks even in populations with relatively high vaccination coverage [@guerra2007]. Importantly, there is increasing recognition that routine immunization programs should evaluate both vaccination coverage and vaccination timeliness. Recent studies have therefore advocated for reporting age-specific vaccination coverage and timeliness indicators to provide a more complete assessment of program performance and to better identify populations at increased risk of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks [@wariri2022; @clark2026].

Previous studies have extensively investigated socioeconomic determinants of vaccination timeliness [@masters2019], while research on climate-sensitive determinants has remained limited. Existing studies examining heat and health have primarily focused on mortality, morbidity and healthcare utilisation, with little evidence on routine childhood vaccination and none on vaccination timeliness in Africa. As climate change continues to increase the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, understanding whether these events influence childhood immunization has important implications for vaccination programs and climate adaptation planning [@siddiqi2025; @zheng2026].

## Aims and Objectives

The aim of this study is to examine the association between heatwave exposure and the timeliness of routine childhood vaccination among children aged 0-36 months in Nigeria.

The specific objectives are as follows:

1.  Estimate the spatial and temporal distribution of heatwave occurrence across Nigeria during 2021–2024.

2.  Estimate the timeliness of the BCG, Pentavalent 1–3 and MCV1 vaccination.

3.  Assess the association of heatwaves and vaccine timeliness while adjusting for selected socioeconomic and demographic characteristics.
